newsitem.title: CHINA: China hails Australia anti-dumping rethink.
newsitem.headline: China hails Australia anti-dumping rethink.

text.p: Beijing on Wednesday hailed Australian moves to treat China as a transition economy, saying Canberra's new flexibility was a significant victory in the fight against anti-dumping laws aimed at Chinese exports.
Australia this month announced it would move to revamp anti-dumping laws to allow closer investigation of individual cases and to treat China as in transition from state planning to a market economy.

"This is a major breakthrough in China's work to deal with anti-dumping charges," crowed the International Business Daily, the mouthpiece newspaper of China's Ministry of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation.

Canberra's decision to rethink its anti-dumping policies had been prompted by the efforts of 15 Chinese companies to contest an anti-dumping suit brought against chemical imports by an Australian firm, the newspaper said in a front page report.

China's Foreign Minstry, Ministry of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation, State Council and Ministry of Chemical Industry had given strong support to efforts to combat the suit, allowing work to go smoothly, it said.

Under previous Australian rules that treated China as a planned economy, the prices of equivalent goods in a third "substitute country" were used to judge whether Chinese imports were being properly valued or dumped.

Some Western economic analysts argue that much of China's production of export goods remains highly subsidised by the state, despite nearly 20 years of market-style reforms that have transformed a strictly managed Stalinist-style economy.

Beijing has repeatedly condemned anti-dumping actions by Australia, the European Union and the United States as a form of covert protectionism, saying cheaper labour and other low costs enable Chinese firms to undercut Western competitors.
Trade policies that treated China as a planned economy were unjustified and unfair, the International Business Daily said.
"These kinds of discriminatory policies cannot but greatly increase the difficulties of Chinese enterprises responding (to anti-dumping actions)," the newspaper said in an editorial.
Canberra's decision to treat China as a transition economy and to deal with anti-dumping issues on a case-by-case basis was good news, but much more needed to be done, it said.

"This is still a distance away from full acceptance of China as a market economy and abandonment of the unfair practice of using substitute countries (for pricing)," it said. "We must still continue to work hard in many areas.
